title: Why do histories of environmental change become anthropocentric memories? Remembering French nuclear tests in the Pacific
abstract: To foster greater pro-environmentalism, recent work in collective memory studies extends frames of remembering to nonhuman losses and suffering – yet dominant memory cultures remain stubbornly anthropocentric. This article explains persisting anthropocentrism by focusing on the narrative architecture of collective memory. Based on structuralist narratology, it argues that anthropocentrism is embedded in master narratives that organise the past around human protagonists and identity-affirming plots. The argument is developed through a case study of how French nuclear testing in the Pacific is remembered in New Zealand. Although the tests caused profound environmental harm, analysis of a variety of memory texts from film, advertising and museums shows that this history is repeatedly narrated through an anthropocentric underdog plot centred on New Zealand’s self-image of ‘a small nation punching above its weight’. The article concludes that making space for ecocentric remembering requires confronting the master narratives through which social groups make the historical past meaningful.
